the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

In our study, we established partnerships with three schools on a large Northern Plains reservation to conduct a comprehensive cross-sectional social network survey among 9th- and 10th-grade students.
We employed Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to model the probability of friendship tie formation within each school
Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model, indicating a robust tendency for mutual friendship nominations.
Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample.
Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools, indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation.
AI identity was largely unassociated with sending or receiving ties, with only a borderline positive receiver effect in School C.
Alcohol use showed significant homophily in School B (AME = 0.0039, p < 0.01) but not in the other schools or for other substances.
